entities.name: Marco Girolamo Vida
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marco Girolamo Vida, born around 1485 in Cremona, Italy, and dying on October 7, 1566, was a pivotal Italian humanist, bishop of Alba, and an architect of Christian Latin literature during the High Renaissance. His sophisticated classical verse, characterized by its Virgilian elegance, sought to reconcile ancient poetic forms with Christian themes, thereby influencing the development of Neo-Latin poetry and solidifying the literary prestige of the Catholic Church in the wake of the Reformation. His career spanned a period of intense intellectual and religious ferment, bridging the classical revival with the Counter-Reformation's cultural agenda, and positioning him as a significant figure in the European literary landscape.

Vida's most celebrated work is the *Christiad*, an epic poem in six books detailing the life of Jesus Christ, published in 1535 and dedicated to Pope Clement VII, who had previously patronized Vida. This ambitious work, composed in polished Latin hexameters, aimed to provide a Christian epic worthy of comparison to Virgil's *Aeneid*, and became a foundational text for later religious epics. Equally influential was his *De arte poetica* (1527), a didactic poem offering comprehensive advice on poetic composition, imitation of classical models, and the moral responsibilities of a poet. He also penned *Scacchia ludus* (The Game of Chess, c. 1513), a lively and witty poem describing a chess match between Apollo and Mercury, which became exceptionally popular, translated into many languages, and contributed significantly to the genre of descriptive poetry.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Marco Girolamo Vida's *De arte poetica* profoundly shaped European literary theory for centuries, directly influencing major figures like Alexander Pope. His *Christiad* also set a benchmark for Christian epic poetry, demonstrating the enduring power of classical forms in sacred contexts.
